steps.title: Как это работает
steps.html:
Разница в том, когда принято решение, а не когда произойдёт действие. Обе формы говорят об одном и том же будущем.

Для прогноза подходят обе. Going to — когда доказательство перед глазами: She's going to fall (она уже качается). Will — когда это ваше мнение: I think she'll be fine.

Для договорённости со временем, местом и другим человеком естественнее Present Continuous: We're meeting the guide at nine.

steps.sub: Why do you think they do it?

steps.title: Living on the water
steps.html:
Around the world, people are moving off the land — not because they want an adventure, but because the land is running out.

A  On Lake Titicaca, high in the Andes, there are islands you can pull apart with your hands. The Uros people build them from reeds, layer on layer, and add fresh reeds on top every few weeks as the bottom rots away. A well-kept island will last about thirty years. There are no cliffs, no rocks and no valleys here — just a flat green landscape that moves slightly underfoot, and about two thousand inhabitants who have lived this way for centuries.

B  Four thousand miles away, in Amsterdam, a very different community is doing something similar for very modern reasons. The city has run out of space. Prices in the suburbs are impossible, and moving inland is not an option, so about a hundred households have settled down on the water instead. Their homes are permanent and connected to the city like any other: post, internet, solar power on the roof.

C  Marijke has lived on one of them for six years. “People think we are going to feel cramped, packed in like sardines,” she says. “Come and look.” Inside, the rooms are ordinary; there is a communal garden shared by the whole block and a thirty-minute ferry service to the mainland. “The one thing you learn is to make room. Everything you own has to earn its place. I’ll never go back to a house with an attic full of things I have forgotten about.”

D  Not everybody is convinced. Building on water is expensive, and critics argue that the money will always go where the profit is. In the Maldives, a company is developing artificial islands to provide housing for the country’s poorer citizens, and by 2030 it expects twenty thousand people to be living there. Others say the same technology will end up producing luxury housing for people who could live anywhere they liked.

E  What is certain is that the pressure is not going to disappear. By 2050, roughly two thirds of the world’s population will live in cities, and a large number of the biggest ones sit on a coast or a river. Some of them will build upwards. Some will build outwards, into the suburbs. A few, planners think, will build onto the water — not as an experiment, but because there will be nowhere else to put people.

F  Marijke is more modest about it. She did not set off six years ago to solve a global problem; she wanted a home she could afford within reach of her work. “I don’t think everyone is going to live like this,” she says. “But you get used to it very fast. After about a month, you stop noticing that the floor is moving. And then it is just where you live.”

Written for this course. Details of the Uros islands, the Amsterdam floating districts and the Maldives project are drawn from published municipal planning documents and UNESCO reporting.

C  Marijke has lived on one of them for six years. “People think we are going to feel cramped, packed in like sardines,” she says. “Come and look.” Inside, the rooms are ordinary; there is a communal garden shared by the whole block and a thirty-minute ferry service to the mainland. “The one thing you learn is to make room. Everything you own has to earn its place. I’ll never go back to a house with an attic full of things I have forgotten about.”

Others say the same technology will end up producing luxury housing for people who could live anywhere they liked.

By 2050, roughly two thirds of the world’s population will live in cities, and a large number of the biggest ones sit on a coast or a river. Some of them will build upwards. She did not set off six years ago to solve a global problem; she wanted a home she could afford within reach of her work. “I don’t think everyone is going to live like this,” she says. “But you get used to it very fast. After about a month, you stop noticing that the floor is moving. And then it is just where you live.”
